extracted.intended_audience: readers and commentators on public policy and political economy (policymakers, journalists, informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for assessing public-economic interventions (taxes, public works, trade restrictions, machinery) by exposing visible effects and the hidden consequences that critics overlook. Emphasises opportunity costs, displacement vs net gain, and the role of intermediaries and technological change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both 'that which is seen' and 'that which is not seen'
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the question in both its elements: the visible effects of an action ('that which is seen') and the hidden or deferred effects ('that which is not seen'). A public enterprise is 'a coin with two sides' — one side shows a labourer at work (seen), the other a labourer out of work (not seen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always state not only the destination given by the State to voted millions but also the destination which the tax-payer would have given; apply this dual view to taxes, public works, intermediaries, restrictions, and machinery. Examples: public works employ visible workers but deprive others of work; legislation that benefits one producer harms consumers and other producers (three-party analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake displacement for net gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat transfers or redistributions (displacements of spending or wages) as additions to national wealth — 'they have exposed themselves to ridicule by mistaking a displacement for a gain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proponents point to wages paid or salaries gained as proof of national gain, check where the funds came from and what other gratifications or wages were reduced. Example: a theatre salary raised at taxpayers' expense displaces pay elsewhere and does not add to the working class's total share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove the utility of taxes by root reasons, not by asserting 'public expenses support the working classes.'
rubrics_metrics.description: When taxes are discussed you must prove their utility by reasons from the root of the matter, not by the assertion 'The public expenses support the working classes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That assertion disguises that public expenses supersede private expenses and substitute one livelihood for another without increasing the total. Demand underlying economic justification, not rhetorical claims about creating employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify public works by real utility, not by the argument 'it creates labour'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a railroad or bridge is of real utility, mention that utility; if not, the justification 'We must find work for the workmen' is a mystification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the project yields benefits to users and society beyond simply hiring workers. Treat emergency, temporary interventions differently (see separate criterion). Examples of abuses: making and unmaking drains purely to create work; Napoleon's alleged ditches example.

rubrics_metrics.name: When evaluating public projects, account for taxpayers' foregone uses (opportunity cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: While stating the destination given by the State to funds, also state the destination which the taxpayer would have given but cannot now give — a public enterprise displaces private uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the counterfactual: what consumption or investment did the taxed person forgo? Example: moving 60,000 francs to theatres displaces other purchases and wages elsewhere; the net effect on national labour may be zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish temporary/emergency public employment from permanent systematic public employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary measures in an emergency (hard winter) may have use as they act like securities and reallocate labour to times of difficulty; as a permanent, general, systematic measure they are 'a ruinous mystification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow limited, short-term public employment to meet crises; reject arguments for sustained permanent public employment justified solely on 'creating work' grounds because they mask displacement and loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the legitimate service of intermediates (merchants, bankers, traders) rather than labeling them parasites
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consists of public services and private services; intermediates (capitalists, bankers, merchants) interpose between production and consumption to organise exchange, information, transport — these are voluntary services with presumptive utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critics denounce intermediates as extortionists, require analysis of what services they render: gathering information, transporting goods, economising costs via competition, and distributing goods to highest-demand areas. Compare three possible arrangements for provisioning (consumers fetch goods themselves, merchants do it, or the State does it) and note why voluntary intermediaries are generally preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate proposals to replace markets with State organisation by comparing total costs, inefficiencies, and abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: If the State replaces commerce, ask where savings would occur — would fewer ships, sailors, or expenses be needed? Would officials work without pay? Would levying taxes and dividing provisions be fair and efficient? Such replacement likely raises costs and invites abuse and responsibility burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand concrete accounting of administrative costs, incentives, and potential for injustice/abuse before accepting proposals to nationalise distribution or provisioning; use the Odessa/corn example to illustrate likely inefficiencies and higher costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: When assessing trade restrictions, account for all affected parties and the 'third person' left out of partial analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions (prohibiting foreign goods) may benefit a protected producer but cause losses to consumers and to other parts of national industry; the usual fallacy is to consider only the producer and the protected worker, omitting the consumer (the 'third person').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply three-party accounting (protected producer gains, consumer loses the price difference, and national industry loses potential alternative spending). Example: M. Prohibant's tariff raises his price but James B. loses purchasing power and shifts spending away from other trades; net national labour is not increased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise legal plunder — law can create redistributional gains at others' expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation that grants privileges (e.g., prohibiting Belgian iron) accomplishes by law what private violence would (plunder) and produces the same economic effects: a profit to the privileged and losses elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize laws that create privileges: are they simply redirecting wealth from one group to another without producing net value? Use moral as well as economic judgment: 'To take by violence is not to produce, but to destroy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not condemn machinery per se; evaluate machines by their unseen productive effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The cry 'A curse on machines!' mistakes visible displacement of workers for the total effect; behind the seen dismissal lies an unseen franc saved that employs other hands or lowers prices benefiting consumers and wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace savings from machinery: the inventor/capitalist may reap initial gains, competition tends to transfer benefits to consumers, and saved funds create employment elsewhere. Assess both short-term displacements and longer-run reallocations and consumption effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess inventions' full effects: savings create funds that sustain wages and new production
rubrics_metrics.description: A new machine lowers production costs; the franc saved does not vanish but becomes available to employ other workmen or to lower prices (benefiting consumers), thus replacing the labour the machine made unnecessary — 'an increase of advantages for equal labour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring the impact of technology, account for how cost reductions reallocate spending and create new demand; avoid relying only on consumption-growth arguments (they can be inconclusive) and instead track the fund of wages sustained by savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic statistical/demand reasoning about machinery and consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that machinery harms labour because consumption of the produced good may not rise proportionally (e.g., hats) are incomplete; even without increased consumption of that good, savings circulate to other trades and secure wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer net harm from static consumption of a single good. Instead analyze how savings reallocate across the economy (new purchases, better living, other trades), using examples like cheaper newspapers freeing funds for other spending.
